items.title: Multidisciplinary attitudes towards LLM-structured oncologic CT reports: a prospective fixed-sequence questionnaire study
items.abstract: Abstract Objectives Large language models (LLMs) can automate the conversion of radiologic free text into structured reports, but multidisciplinary reader preferences for the resulting output remain insufficiently studied. This prospective, two-phase, fixed-sequence within-participant study evaluated reader assessments of LLM-structured versus conventional free-text oncologic CT reports. Material & Methods A paired convenience sample of radiologists, radiology technologists, oncologists, and medical students was recruited between May and November 2025. In Phase 1, participants rated 5 free-text oncologic CT reports for readability and comprehension (3 items), oncologic information quality (5 items), and clinical utility (4 items) on a 9-point Likert scale. After a washout of at least 4 weeks, participants rated the LLM-structured version generated by Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct. Results Sixty-six paired participants (24 medical students, 22 radiologists, 12 radiology technologists, 8 oncologists) were included (mean [standard deviation] age, 30.5 [7.6] years; 37 [56.1%] female). Structured reports showed significantly higher odds of agreement for 11 of 12 items (odds ratio [OR] range, 1.70–4.81), with strongest effects for clinical utility (OR, 4.81; 95% CI, 3.24–7.15), information findability (OR, 4.31; 95% CI, 3.12–5.96), recommendation clarity (OR, 4.14; 95% CI, 2.95–5.83), and patient communication suitability (OR, 3.45; 95% CI, 2.59–4.60). Radiology technologists showed significantly higher ratings for all 12 items, radiologists for 6, students for 7, and oncologists for none. Conclusion In this single-center paired sample, LLM-structured oncologic CT reports received higher reader ratings than conventional free-text reports across most evaluated dimensions, with the largest differences observed for information findability and clinical utility. These findings support further evaluation of radiologist-supervised LLM-assisted report structuring, including formal source-to-output validation and randomized multicenter assessment, before clinical implementation.

items.title: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence for Social Media Content Verification, Influence Assessment and Risk Analysis
items.abstract: Social platforms now carry news, opinion, commerce and public safety information in a blend of text, pictures, video and audio. Deception has adapted to this format: a genuine photograph can be given a false caption, a synthetic voice can be attached to an old clip, and coordinated accounts can push a post until it looks popular. Detectors that examine only one channel often miss these cases. This paper presents a unified multimodal framework that treats three linked questions together: is the content authentic (verification), who and what is amplifying it (influence), and how much harm could it cause (risk). The framework encodes each modality separately, aligns them through cross-modal attention, and feeds a shared representation to three task heads whose outputs are merged into an interpretable risk score with a human review step. We survey existing work, describe the architecture, datasets, training approach and evaluation protocol, discuss applications in journalism, public health, brand safety, elections and disaster response, and examine ethical constraints such as privacy, bias and over-blocking. The contribution is a design and evaluation blueprint rather than a new benchmark result, and we close with open problems and a research agenda.

items.title: Nanoenzymes and Cancer Therapy: Current Perspectives
items.abstract: Over the past fifteen years, nanozymes—artificial nanomaterials with enzyme-like catalytic activity—have evolved from a laboratory phenomenon into one of the most rapidly advancing platforms in nanomedicine. The unique ability of nanozymes to selectively modulate the levels of reactive oxygen species within the tumor microenvironment opens fundamentally new avenues for highly selective therapy of malignant neoplasms. This review systematically presents current advances in the development of "smart" nanozymes for cancer treatment. Catalytic mechanisms are discussed in detail, including peroxidase-like, oxidase-like, catalase-like, superoxide dismutase-like, and hydrolase-like activities, as well as the factors influencing these processes. The main classes of nanozymes are analyzed: metals and metal oxides, carbon-based materials, metal-organic frameworks, single-atom catalysts, bimetallic and biomimetic systems. Strategies for enhancing catalytic efficiency are examined: heterometallic doping, defect engineering, surface modification, control of porosity and dimensionality, and the use of hybrid constructs with natural enzymes. Special attention is given to the integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning methods for predicting nanozyme structure and activity, thereby accelerating the search for optimal candidates. Therapeutic modalities are described—chemodynamic, photothermal, photodynamic, and sonodynamic therapy, depletion therapy, immunotherapy, as well as the induction of novel forms of cell death. It is shown that combined approaches, in which nanozymes perform multiple catalytic functions simultaneously, are the most effective. Finally, barriers to clinical translation are critically assessed: long-term biosafety, incomplete in vivo specificity, the challenge of scalable synthesis, and the lack of standardized evaluation protocols. Potential strategies to overcome these limitations are proposed.

items.title: Natural Language Query Hybrid Architecture for Cross-Sectoral Analytics Dashboards on Public Statistical Data
items.abstract: Background: Public statistical data are essential for evidence-based policymaking, yet the complexity of cross-sectoral indicators often limits accessibility for nontechnical users. This challenge is particularly relevant in East Java, where regional development disparities require integrated analytical tools. Objective: This study aims to develop a cross-sectoral analytics dashboard integrating Natural Language Query (NLQ), Apriori association-rule mining, and a supporting local large language model (LLM). Methods: The system was developed using the SDLC Waterfall model and utilized more than 50 Statistics Indonesia (BPS) indicators covering 38 districts/cities in East Java from 2016 to 2026. A deterministic, rule- and regular-expression (regex)-based Text-to-SQL mechanism processed natural-language queries, while Apriori identified cross-sectoral association patterns. A local LLM (Ollama, llama3.2:1b) generated supporting narratives. Evaluation included black-box testing, 50-query intent classification, association-rule metrics, and an exploratory LLM assessment. Results: The NLQ module achieved 96.00% accuracy (48/50 queries). Apriori generated 55,480 high-level rules with an average confidence of 0.909 and lift of 15.44. The exploratory LLM evaluation achieved a composite score of 4.35/5.00, a 2.5% hallucination rate, a 26.07-second P95 latency, and a 100% fallback success rate. Conclusion: The hybrid architecture effectively supports accessible statistical-data retrieval and cross-sectoral pattern discovery, while the LLM remains a supporting narrative component that requires further formal validation.

items.title: Natural, Artificial, and Human Intelligences
items.abstract: Human achievement, whether in culture, science, or technology, is unparalleled in the known existence. This achievement is tied to the enormous communities of knowledge, made possible by language. We trace how the principle ‘᾿Eν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος’ (in the beginning was the word) was extended beyond its theological origins and heightened the value of written intelligence throughout Western societies. There lies the challenge regarding modern-age chatbots: they can ‘do’ language apparently as well as ourselves, and there is a natural question of whether they can be considered intelligent, in the same way as we are or otherwise. Are humans uniquely intelligent? We consider this question in terms of the psychological literature on intelligence, evidence for intelligence in non-human animals, the role of written language in science and technology, progress with artificial intelligence, the history of intelligence testing (for both humans and machines), and the role of embodiment in intelligence. We think that it is increasingly difficult to consider humans uniquely intelligent. There are current limitations in chatbots, e.g., concerning perceptual and social awareness, but much attention is currently devoted to overcoming such limitations.

items.title: Non-medical drivers of health and pediatric no-show prediction: identifying modifiable risk factors
items.abstract: Abstract Background No-shows to medical appointments contribute to disruptions and inefficiencies in healthcare delivery. While artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML) models are increasingly used to predict no-shows, few have incorporated non-medical drivers of health (NMDOH), particularly in pediatric populations. This study evaluated the inclusion of NMDOH in pediatric AI/ML no-show prediction and identified modifiable factors associated with no-shows. Methods A retrospective study was conducted of scheduled pediatric appointments across six general pediatrics clinics during April–August 2024 using electronic health record and NMDOH screening data. A transformer-based AI/ML no-show model was evaluated using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC). Multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate factors associated with no-show status. Results Among 7,931 included appointments, 2761 (34.8%) were no-shows. Models with and without NMDOH variables showed similar performance (AUROC 0.708 for both; AUPRC 0.536 vs. 0.535, respectively). Inclusion of patient demographic and insurance variables produced a small improvement in performance, with similar results with and without NMDOH inclusion (AUROC 0.721 and AUPRC 0.542 for both). No-shows were associated with unconfirmed appointments, non-active patient portal status, transportation needs, and housing instability. Conclusions NMDOH variables did not significantly change model performance but identified actionable factors associated with no-shows. Prediction models may be most useful when paired with targeted outreach and barrier-reduction strategies. Impact Non-medical drivers of health (NMDOH), including transportation needs and housing instability, as well as appointment confirmation and patient portal activation, were associated with missed pediatric appointments. Inclusion of NMDOH in AI/ML no-show prediction models did not meaningfully change prediction performance. The associations highlight modifiable barriers that can be targeted through clinical and operational interventions. AI-based no-show prediction may be most effective when paired with outreach and barrier-reduction strategies.

items.title: Occupational Exposure Limits for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients: A Comparative Review of ICH Q3C, OSHA, NIOSH, and European Medicines Agency Regulatory Frameworks and their Implications for Worker Health Surveillance
items.abstract: Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) pose a significant occupational health challenge in pharmaceutical manufacturing and healthcare settings, where workers involved in synthesis, formulation, packaging, dispensing, and administration may be exposed to pharmacologically potent substances. Occupational Exposure Limits (OELs) are essential for protecting workers from unintended biological effects. This review critically evaluates four regulatory frameworks relevant to pharmaceutical occupational exposure: ICH Q3C on residual solvents, Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) Permissible Exposure Limits (PELs), National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) Recommended Exposure Limits (RELs), and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) guideline for health-based exposure limits (HBELs). Their scientific foundations, derivation methodologies, applicability, legal status, and implications for occupational health surveillance were compared. A literature search was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and regulatory databases, including OSHA, NIOSH, EMA, ICH, and ISPE, covering publications from 1990 to 2024. Studies addressing OEL derivation, occupational exposure assessment, worker health outcomes, and regulatory compliance were narratively synthesised. Considerable heterogeneity was identified among frameworks regarding scientific basis, methodology, update frequency, and enforceability. ICH Q3C provides classifications and permitted daily exposure limits for residual solvents but is not specifically designed for API dust. OSHA PELs is legally enforceable but include numerous limits that have not been comprehensively updated. NIOSH RELs incorporate scientific evidence but are generally advisory. EMA HBEL methodology offers an API-specific approach based on pharmacological and toxicological evaluation, although its primary regulatory purpose is prevention of cross-contamination. Occupational Exposure Banding (OEB) approaches, including ISPE systems, provide practical support where substance-specific OELs are unavailable. Overall, no single framework fully addresses pharmaceutical occupational health needs. Greater international harmonisation, periodic review, exposure monitoring, and health surveillance are needed to strengthen worker protection. Major Findings: Regulatory frameworks differ substantially in scope, legal status, and scientific basis for API occupational exposure. EMA HBEL/PDE, NIOSH, and ISPE OEB approaches provide complementary tools, but no single framework fully addresses worker protection. An integrated OEL/OEB-based exposure assessment, biological monitoring, and proportional health surveillance framework is proposed.

items.title: Occupational Health Perspectives on Depression and Anxiety among Medical, Paramedical, and Non-Medical University Students: A Comparative Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Depression and anxiety are increasingly reported among university students and represent significant concerns for academic performance and psychological well-being. Students enrolled in different academic streams may experience varying levels of psychological distress due to differences in curriculum demands, evaluation pressure, and professional expectations. The present study aimed to compare levels of depression and anxiety among medical, paramedical, and nonmedical university students using baseline (pre-test) data. A total of 180 university students (60 medical, 60 paramedical, and 60 non-medical) participated in this comparative cross-sectional study. Depression and anxiety were assessed using the Depression Anxiety Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21). Descriptive statistics and inferential analyses were conducted to examine stream-wise differences in psychological symptoms. The findings revealed significant differences in levels of depression and anxiety across academic streams, with medical and paramedical students reporting higher levels of psychological distress compared to non-medical students. The results highlight the influence of academic context on student mental health and underscore the need for stream-specific mental health support within higher education institutions. The findings have important occupational health implications by highlighting the need for early mental health promotion and preventive interventions among students preparing for future professional roles. Major Findings: Medical and paramedical students reported significantly higher levels of depression than non-medical students. Anxiety showed significant overall variation across academic streams, although pairwise differences were comparatively modest. The findings emphasize the need for stream-specific mental health interventions and counselling support within higher education institutions.

items.title: OCCUPATIONAL RISK ASSESSMENT IN THE RECEPTION OF AÇAÍ BY SMALL VESSELS ON THE WATERFRONT OF MACAPÁ, AMAPÁ, BRAZIL
items.abstract: This study assessed occupational risks in the reception and manual handling of açaí transported by small vessels at the Açaí Ramp on the waterfront of Macapá, Amapá, Brazil. An applied, qualitative, descriptive, exploratory field study was conducted from August 2025 to September 2026. Data were obtained through in loco technical visits, direct observation of the work process, field records, and a set of 35 photographs used as documentary support. Occupational hazards were grouped as physical, biological, ergonomic, and accident-related, and prioritized through a qualitative 3 × 3 matrix combining probability and severity. The most relevant conditions were manual handling of baskets and sacks, trunk flexion, worker-to-worker load transfer, wet and inclined surfaces, instability at the vessel-ramp interface, proximity to the river, and shared circulation with vehicles and other users. Ergonomic and accident risks reached the highest priority levels, while heat, solar radiation, humidity, and potential contact with wastewater were classified as moderate. No chemical risk was retained because the field evidence was insufficient. Preventive measures focused on engineering and organizational controls, improved drainage, safer transfer conditions, circulation management, auxiliary handling devices, hydration, and appropriate footwear. The study provides a context-specific basis for preventive action in a little-examined stage of the Amazonian açaí supply chain.

items.title: One-Step Stochastically-Assembled Copper(I) Iodide Cluster for Multimodal Physically Unclonable Functions
items.abstract: The rapid development of the Internet of Things and artificial intelligence has sharply increased the demand for secure, low-cost, and scalable anticounterfeiting technologies. Physical unclonable functions (PUFs) offer intrinsic protection by converting stochastic material variations into unique identifiers, but their practical implementation is often limited by complex fabrication, toxic luminophores, and low information complexity arising from single-channel readout. Here, we develop a copper(I) iodide cluster-poly(methyl methacrylate) fluorescent PUF through a single ambient coating step. Nonequilibrium solvent evaporation and polymer solidification generate randomly distributed yellow-emissive microdomains together with three-dimensional surface relief, while the cluster and polymer concentrations regulate domain coverage, intensity, and morphology without prescribing their microscopic arrangement. Binary fluorescence keys exhibit a mean interlabel Hamming distance of 0.49935 and an intralabel value of 0.00219. Incorporating discretized surface height further enables multivalued fluorescence-topography encoding. The solution-processable composite is compatible with spin coating, spray coating, transfer printing, and direct writing, allowing stochastic fingerprints to be integrated into planar, flexible, and curved objects for diverse anticounterfeiting scenarios. The fingerprints remain readable after storage, water exposure, thermal treatment, and ultraviolet irradiation. Deep-learning retrieval combined with local-feature matching enables hierarchical identification and physical verification. This work provides a simple, lead-free route to multimodal PUFs for scalable anticounterfeiting and authentication.

items.title: Online Teaching and Learning in South Asian Higher Education: Challenges and Emerging Opportunities for Teacher Education and Physical Education
items.abstract: Abstract Online teaching and learning has become a permanent component of higher education, yet its educational value depends on more than access to digital platforms. This critical integrative review examines the development of online higher education in South Asia and focuses specifically on its implications for teacher education and physical education. Drawing on recent regional reports, peer-reviewed reviews, policy documents and foundational theories of online learning, the review synthesises evidence concerning digital inequality, faculty competence, learner engagement, assessment, academic integrity, artificial intelligence, accessibility and quality assurance. The analysis shows that South Asian institutions have moved from pandemic-era emergency remote teaching toward a more complex phase of sustainable digital transformation, but progress remains uneven across countries and institutions. Teacher education requires explicit development of digital pedagogical competence, authentic assessment and supervised professional practice, while physical education requires a discipline-sensitive blended model because embodied, psychomotor and safety-related outcomes cannot be fully reproduced online. Generative AI offers emerging opportunities for personalised learning, feedback, multilingual support and professional development, but it also introduces risks related to privacy, bias, academic integrity and over-reliance. The review proposes a Context-Responsive Online Teaching and Learning Framework built around infrastructure readiness, pedagogical alignment, faculty competence, learner support, inclusive access, authentic assessment, discipline-sensitive design and responsible innovation. The article argues that the future of online higher education in South Asia should not be defined by the quantity of technology adopted, but by the quality, equity and educational purpose with which technology is integrated. Keywords: Online Higher Education; South Asia; Teacher Education; Physical Education; Generative Artificial Intelligence. items.title: Opportunities and Challenges from Artificial Intelligence in Public Service Delivery in Vietnam
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on public service delivery in Vietnam, thereby proposing some key policy implications for Vietnam. This study employs a narrative literature review approach. The results show that AI offers opportunities to improve the quality of public service delivery, expand access to services, and support civil servants in handling their work. However, challenges exist stemming from the limitations of AI itself, the lack of a shared digital data platform, the shortage of human resources, and the lack of necessary funding. The study proposes policy implications for developing a "hybrid" model of public service communication between humans and machines, focusing on building digital databases, enhancing the digital capacity of civil servants, increasing state budget allocation, and expanding the mobilization of resources from society and internationally.

items.title: Optical Flow–Derived Motion Biomarkers and Explainable Artificial Intelligence for Quantitative Assessment of Robotic Surgical Expertise
items.abstract: Background Objective surgical skill evaluation remains challenging in robotic-assisted surgery. Existing artificial intelligence frameworks often depend on robotic telemetry or “black-box” deep learning models that reduce interpretability and translational accessibility. Methods The present study developed an interpretable computer vision framework for quantitative analysis of robotic surgical motion using dense optical flow–derived biomarkers extracted directly from surgical video recordings. Robotic suturing videos from the publicly available JIGSAWS dataset were analyzed using a Python/OpenCV-based pipeline. Quantitative motion biomarkers, including motion magnitude, temporal variability, jerk-related parameters, and smoothness indices, were extracted and evaluated across expert, intermediate, and novice surgical groups. The paired left and right stereo views were averaged to produce one feature vector for each independent trial. Statistical comparisons were performed using the Kruskal–Wallis test. Skill classification was evaluated using a class-weighted Random Forest classifier with Leave-One-User-Out cross-validation. Model predictions were interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Results Optical flow analysis successfully extracted reproducible motion biomarkers associated with surgical expertise. Significant differences were observed in mean motion magnitude ( P = .0035), mean absolute jerk ( P = .00074), and the unnormalized smoothness index ( P = .00074). Motion variability did not differ significantly among the groups after trial-level aggregation ( P = .0769). SPARC showed the expected ordering of normalized smoothness, with the highest values among experts, but the group difference was not statistically significant ( P = .0647). Principal component analysis demonstrated partial clustering of surgical expertise groups based on extracted motion dynamics. Under Leave-One-User-Out cross-validation, the Random Forest classifier achieved an overall accuracy of 38.5%, a balanced accuracy of 29.5%, a macro-average AUC of 0.401, and a weighted-average AUC of 0.430. Genuine out-of-fold SHAP analysis identified the smoothness index, mean absolute jerk, and mean absolute acceleration as the largest contributors to the model outputs. Conclusions Optical flow–derived motion biomarkers provide an interpretable characterization of robotic surgical movement directly from video recordings without requiring robotic telemetry. However, the modest performance under user-independent validation indicates that these biomarkers should not yet be used as a standalone measure of surgical expertise. The proposed framework provides a transparent basis for developing and externally validating video-based surgical skill assessment methods.

items.title: Organizational and legal principles of the use of artificial intelligence in the process of exercising the constitutional right to higher education in Ukraine
items.abstract: The purpose of the article is to provide a comprehensive characterization of the current organizational and legal framework for the use of artificial intelligence in the exercise of the constitutional right to higher education in Ukraine, to identify problems associated with the implementation of its regulatory potential, and to formulate proposals for optimizing the regulatory framework governing the use of artificial intelligence by higher education students in the learning process. The scientific analysis of the organizational and legal framework for the use of artificial intelligence in the exercise of the constitutional right to higher education in Ukraine was conducted using a system of general and specific methods of scientific inquiry. The dialectical philosophical and legal approach served as the basic methodological foundation for the development of the empirical material of the article. Among the general methods of scientific inquiry, the method of ascending from the abstract to the concrete, the systemic and structural method, and the systemic and functional method were applied. Among the specific methods of scientific inquiry, the method of legal formalization, the historical and legal method, and the method of theoretical and legal forecasting were employed. A comprehensive scientific analysis of the organizational and legal framework for the use of artificial intelligence in the exercise of the constitutional right to higher education in Ukraine demonstrated that the provisions of current education legislation do not establish clear legal frameworks for its use by higher education students. It was established that, within the current system of national legislation of Ukraine, there is no law that defines clear legal parameters for the status of artificial intelligence technologies and the rules governing their use (application) in various spheres of social life and public administration, including higher education. The authors substantiate the position that the use of artificial intelligence products by higher education students takes place within the exercise of the constitutionally guaranteed right to use various forms and methods of learning, as well as the right to free access to information for educational purposes in accessible formats through the use of competitive technologies while participating in scientific, innovative, and research and technological activities. It was established that, against the background of the absence of legislation regulating the use of artificial intelligence in education, a general trend among Ukrainian higher education institutions has been attempts to regulate, at the local level, the use of relevant technologies by participants in the educational process. The results of the scientific study of the selected issue make it possible to conclude that the lack of regulatory and legal provisions governing the rules and procedures for the use of artificial intelligence technologies in higher education increases the risks of artificial intelligence having a harmful impact on the quality of knowledge acquired at higher education institutions. Taking this into account, as well as in the context of Ukraine’s accelerated European integration, amendments to the fundamental legislative acts governing higher education are proposed in order to establish generally binding rules for the use of artificial intelligence in the exercise of the right to higher education in Ukraine. A promising area for further research is the development of well-substantiated proposals concerning the content of the relevant amendments and the forecasting of their regulatory impact following their implementation.

items.title: Overview and Assessment of Ship Emissions Estimation Models
items.abstract: Abstract This review provides a comprehensive comparative assessment of ship emissions estimation models across the various ship emissions estimation modelling approaches, with a focus on key approaches: top-down, bottom-up, hybrid approaches, and emerging machine learning and artificial intelligence-based techniques as an innovative approach, offering new perspectives and solutions for the maritime industry through its powerful data analysis and pattern recognition capabilities. It delves into important ship emissions estimation models that use advanced data-driven techniques, ranging from simplified to complex, which are continually evolving to improve accuracy by incorporating real-time data, technological advancements, and the impact of environmental policies. Afterwards, this review provides an overall analysis of the ship emissions models, highlighting current research gaps in data availability and quality, challenges in selecting ship emissions estimation methods, and future research topics. Finally, it concludes with future directions in advanced machine learning methods, digital twins, advanced sensor integration, and global monitoring for precise forecasting and regulatory support, all of which are crucial for decarbonization targets.

items.title: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning of SAM for SAR flood mapping: comparative performance and encoder–decoder representation analysis
items.abstract: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) enables flood mapping under cloud and adverse weather, but segmentation remains challenging across heterogeneous environments. Deep-learning models can improve flood delineation, yet their dependence on task-specific training data limits transfer across regions and events. This motivates adapting pretrained vision foundation models to SAR despite the domain gap from RGB imagery. Among these models, we use the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to compare five parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) strategies, comprising Adapter, Prefix tuning, Prompt tuning, BitFit and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), under a consistent prompting protocol across four held-out test scenes and repeated training configurations. All PEFT strategies outperform unadapted SAM, with flood-class IoU ranging from 32.26% to 57.94% and F1 scores from 46.72% to 69.17%. A hybrid LoRA-BitFit configuration achieves the highest overall IoU and F1, while LoRA favours recall and BitFit precision. Encoder–decoder representation analysis further shows that LoRA and LoRA-BitFit strengthen flood/non-flood separability in the image encoder, whereas LoRA-BitFit maintains high attention-weight separability across several later mask-decoder stages. These results show that SAR adaptation depends not simply on the number of trainable parameters, but on which model components are modified and how adaptation is distributed across the encoder–decoder architecture.

items.title: PARAPHRASING MACHINES AND ACADEMIC INTEGRITY: INDONESIAN EFL STUDENTS' USE OF DIGITAL TOOLS TO AVOID PLAGIARISM IN THESIS WRITING
items.abstract: Paraphrasing is central to avoiding plagiarism in thesis writing, yet many EFL students find it difficult and increasingly hand it to digital tools. This study examines how Indonesian EFL students use digital tools to avoid plagiarism in thesis writing and what their practices reveal about their understanding of academic integrity. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design combined a questionnaire completed by 23 undergraduate, master's and doctoral students from 11 universities with semi-structured interviews with six of them. Students rated paraphrasing as one of the harder language skills (M = 2.96 on a scale where 1 is very difficult), and 22 of 23 used online tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly or thesauruses. Of the 20 students who described how they avoid plagiarism, 9 delegated paraphrasing entirely to tools, 3 combined tools with their own editing or translation, 5 relied on their own words and correct citation, 2 used similarity checkers and 1 sought peer feedback. QuillBot was named by 8 students and was the default strategy among doctoral respondents. Interviews revealed premium accounts bought through online marketplaces, tools shared among friends, and one interviewee's observation, from Turnitin training, that similarity checkers cannot verify whether in-text citations match the reference list. The findings suggest that students commonly equate avoiding plagiarism with avoiding textual similarity, a view that treats integrity as a technical matter rather than one of authorship and attribution. The study proposes an integrity-oriented paraphrasing process and discusses implications for supervision, writing instruction and institutional AI policy.

items.title: PEDAGOGICAL POTENTIAL AND LIMITATIONS OF AI TOOLS FOR ACADEMIC WRITING INSTRUCTION
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence tools in higher education has created new opportunities for academic writing instruction while simultaneously raising concerns about learner dependence, authorship, academic integrity, source reliability, and the development of independent thinking. This article examines the pedagogical potential and limitations of AI tools in academic writing instruction from a theoretical and analytical perspective. Particular attention is paid to the use of generative AI for brainstorming, outlining, language support, formative feedback, revision, vocabulary development, and individualized learning. The analysis also considers major limitations, including hallucinated information, fabricated references, overreliance on automated suggestions, homogenization of writing style, reduced cognitive engagement, and difficulties in assessing authentic student performance. The study argues that AI tools are most effective when they function as supplementary pedagogical resources rather than substitutes for student reasoning, source evaluation, and authorship. Effective integration requires clear instructional objectives, process-oriented assessment, AI literacy, transparent disclosure practices, teacher mediation, and systematic verification of AI-generated information. The article concludes that the educational value of AI in academic writing depends less on the technological capabilities of the tools themselves than on the pedagogical framework within which they are used. Keywords: artificial intelligence, academic writing, generative AI, writing instruction, formative feedback, academic integrity, AI literacy, learner autonomy, higher education, writing pedagogy

items.title: Pedagogies of Prompting
items.abstract: The growing integration of generative AI in higher education has positioned prompt literacy as an essential pedagogical competency across disciplines. No longer confined to technical domains, prompting now shapes inquiry, learning, assessment, and knowledge production. This chapter argues for a shift from informal AI use to structured teaching grounded in constructivist, cognitive, and digital literacy frameworks. It explores how prompt literacy can be effectively taught across humanities, social sciences, sciences, and professional fields, emphasizing its role in problem framing, critical thinking, ethical reasoning, and reflective practice. A cross-disciplinary framework is proposed, integrating scaffolding, disciplinary alignment, and ethical engagement. Viewing prompting as dialogic interaction, the chapter highlights its potential to enhance creativity, inquiry, and responsible AI use while addressing risks of superficial learning and inequity.

items.title: Pendampingan Pemanfaatan Media Generatif berbasis Artificial Intelligence dalam Penyusunan Modul Ajar PAI Guru Sekolah Kepulauan
items.abstract: Guru Pendidikan Agama Islam (PAI) di wilayah kepulauan menghadapi tantangan dalam menyusun modul ajar yang sesuai standar Kurikulum Merdeka akibat keterbatasan pemahaman teknologi pendidikan dan tingginya beban kerja administratif. Kegiatan pengabdian kepada masyarakat ini bertujuan mendampingi guru PAI di SMPN Satu Atap 01 Pulau Pari, Kepulauan Seribu, dalam memanfaatkan media generatif berbasis Artificial Intelligence (AI) dengan pendekatan deep learning untuk menyusun dan memvalidasi modul ajar. Kegiatan dilaksanakan pada 11 Mei 2026 melalui tahapan sosialisasi, pelatihan, penerapan teknologi, serta pendampingan dan evaluasi, diikuti oleh guru SD dan SMP di Pulau Pari. Evaluasi program dilakukan melalui survei kepuasan peserta (n=25) yang mencakup dua aspek, yaitu pelaksanaan acara dan kualitas fasilitator. Hasil survei menunjukkan tingkat kepuasan pelaksanaan acara sebesar 87% (Sangat Puas) dan kepuasan terhadap fasilitator sebesar 93% (Sangat Baik), dengan skor tertinggi pada aspek pelayanan panitia dan penguasaan materi oleh fasilitator. Peserta memberikan masukan berupa penambahan contoh praktis, variasi metode, dan perpanjangan sesi diskusi. Temuan ini mengindikasikan bahwa pendekatan pendampingan yang kontekstual dan berbasis praktik efektif membangun penerimaan awal guru terhadap teknologi AI generatif, meskipun keberlanjutan perubahan praktik penyusunan modul ajar memerlukan siklus pendampingan lanjutan. Teachers in island regions face limited access to professional development amid the demands of the Kurikulum Merdeka (Independent Curriculum), which requires the independent and systematic compilation of teaching modules. This community service activity aimed to assist teachers at SMPN Satu Atap 01 Pulau Pari, Thousand Islands, in utilizing artificial intelligence (AI)-based generative media to compile Islamic Religious Education (PAI) teaching modules along with their supporting tools. The activity was carried out on May 11, 2026, through five stages: socialization, training, technology application, mentoring and evaluation, and the completion of evaluation instruments. The evaluation employed a one-group pretest-posttest design involving 24 teachers using a five-item self-efficacy questionnaire on a 1–5 scale, supplemented by data collection on module component completeness, estimated compilation time, and participant satisfaction surveys. The results showed an increase in the average perceived capability score from 2.44 to 4.68 with an N-Gain of 0.88 in the high category, presenting a statistically significant difference (Wilcoxon, p < 0.001). A total of 23 out of 24 participants experienced an increase, and none decreased. All participants produced a complete draft of a teaching module, with 23 of them containing all five complete components ranging from learning objectives to learning media and student worksheets. Furthermore, the estimated compilation time for a single module dropped from a majority taking over three hours to less than one hour. Remaining challenges included system limitations in generating visual illustrations, handling materials with mathematical symbols, and breaking down learning achievements into learning objectives. Recommendations include tiered mentoring, the provision of digital guides and online consultation channels, and expert evaluation of module quality in the next cycle.

items.title: Performance of Large Language Models in Answering Juvenile Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Questions: A Blinded Expert-based Comparative Study
items.abstract: Background: Large language models are increasingly used to obtain medical information, but their performance in juvenile systemic lupus erythematosus remains insufficiently characterized. Objective: To compare expert-rated response quality and clinical relevance across 4 artificial intelligence (AI) models using standardized juvenile systemic lupus erythematosus–related questions. Design: Cross-sectional expert-based comparative study. Setting: Freely accessible consumer-facing web interfaces evaluated on December 30, 2025. Participants: Ten pediatric rheumatology experts. Intervention: Not applicable. Main Outcome Measures: Twenty standardized questions generated 80 AI responses, rated on a 5-point Likert Scale. Model performance was compared using the Friedman test with Kendall W and Bonferroni-corrected post hoc analyses; interrater agreement was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Results: DeepSeek achieved the highest median rating [5 (1 to 5)], followed by Gemini [4 (2 to 5)], ChatGPT [4 (3 to 5)], and Copilot [4 (3 to 5)]. Overall expert-rated performance differed significantly among models [Friedman χ 2 (3) = 63.553, p < 0.001; Kendall W = 0.106]. DeepSeek outperformed ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot (all p < 0.001), while Gemini performed better than ChatGPT ( p = 0.007) and Copilot ( p < 0.001). Interrater agreement was highest for DeepSeek (ICC =0 .734) and lowest for Copilot (ICC = 0.043). Trust scores remained unchanged before and after evaluation [4 (3 to 5) vs. 4 (3 to 5), p =0.414]. Limitation: Single-time-point, single-response testing did not assess within-model reproducibility, and the question set was not formally validated. Conclusion: AI models differed in expert-rated performance and interrater agreement; outputs should be interpreted cautiously and with specialist oversight.

items.title: Phage Therapy and Phage-Derived Lytic Proteins in the One Health Era: Mechanisms, Challenges and Emerging Innovations
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a critical global health threat, as conventional antibiotics are increasingly ineffective against multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogens, particularly ESKAPE organisms. In response, bacteriophages and their derived lytic proteins, including endolysins, holins, and spanins, have emerged as promising therapeutic alternatives. This review examines the comparative therapeutic potential of phages and phage-derived lytic proteins as complementary antibacterial strategies within a One-Health framework, which remains underdeveloped. We explore phage biology, including both lytic and lysogenic cycles, as a mechanistic foundation for understanding their role in addressing the growing threat of antimicrobial resistance. Additionally, we detail bacterial defense mechanisms, such as restriction modification systems, CRISPR-Cas systems, and spontaneous mutations that confer phage resistance. Lytic proteins demonstrate efficacy in treating systemic infections, disrupting biofilm, and targeting resistant pathogens across humans, livestock, and aquaculture. Although phage therapy is a promising antibacterial alternative, it still faces several constraints, including a narrow host range, immune clearance, complex pharmacokinetics, and the inability of exogenous lytic proteins to cross the outer membranes of Gram-negative bacteria. This review highlights emerging solutions to these challenges, including the use of artificial intelligence (AI) for phage and lysin discovery, machine learning models for predicting effective phage combinations, and the engineering of phage lytic proteins to broaden antimicrobial spectra. It also discusses combination strategies that pair whole phages with their derived proteins to exploit synergistic antibacterial effects and counter the emergence of resistance, as well as advanced delivery systems designed to protect phage integrity and enhance activity in hostile physiological environments.

items.title: Physics-Causality-Anchored Verification Theory (PCAVT) · 唯物实践论
items.abstract: Physics-Causality-Anchored Verification Theory (PCAVT) — formerly 唯物实践论 (Material-Praxis Theory) — is a formally constrained category-derivation system that takes carrying natural language (Chinese) as its symbol basis. It treats the Chinese sign system as a set of B1 constants and derives strictly, giving it a mathematical character: non-ambiguous, derivable, and self-consistent. Core outputs include the Three Laws (structural conditions for any shared symbolic system), the A-B-C six-subset framework (A material substrate, B information, C agent), and difference analysis (A2 − A1, the material net output of human practice). The repository publishes the methodology (5th edition), the self-reference-consistency statement, the formalization-alienation critique, and applied papers (economics, gender narrative, education, AI/LLM training-data quality), together with reproducible scripts and figures. This record archives the public repository as a citable research corpus.

items.title: Planning Concerts with AI: An Integrated Decision-Support Framework for Demand, Sustainability, and Economic Feasibility
items.abstract: Concert organizers must balance financial success, operational efficiency, and environmental sustainability, yet these factors are often evaluated separately. Artificial intelligence and workflow automation offer opportunities for integration, but integrated decision-support systems remain limited in concert planning. This study develops an AI-assisted concert-planning decision-support system implemented in n8n. It combines user-defined event parameters with external artist-popularity metrics and currency exchange services to estimate audience demand, environmental indicators, and financial feasibility, and generate structured planning recommendations within one workflow. A case study based on Coldplay’s Music of the Spheres World Tour concert at Olympiastadion Berlin demonstrates the framework’s functionality. The system predicted attendance of 72,306 spectators, approximately 97% of stated venue capacity, and generated planning estimates for energy consumption, carbon emissions, waste, transportation, ticket revenue, costs, and profitability. Because complete verified concert-specific data were unavailable, these outputs demonstrate system functionality and plausibility rather than validate predictive accuracy or reconstruct actual concert performance. The framework illustrates how integrated AI and workflow automation can support efficiency, transparency, and consistency in pre-event decision-making. It also shows how environmental sustainability and economic viability can be assessed together rather than as independent objectives. Intended to support early-stage feasibility assessment, the system does not replace detailed operational analyses or comprehensive life-cycle assessments. It provides a practical approach to more sustainable, transparent, and data-driven planning in the live event industry.

items.title: Platform Justice: Algorithmic Management, Worker Deactivation And Due Process In India's Gig Economy
items.abstract: Digital platforms have changed how work is organised in India. Ride-hailing, food delivery and home services give millions of people an income, yet most of these workers are called “partners”, not employees. Software assigns their tasks, sets incentives, tracks performance and can cut off their access to work, often without explanation. This paper examines algorithmic deactivation: the suspension, blocking or termination of a worker’s access to a platform through automated or partly automated systems. It argues that deactivation is not only a contractual matter. Where platform work is a main source of income, unexplained or arbitrary deactivation raises real questions of fairness, equality, privacy and access to justice. The paper reviews the Code on Social Security, 2020, Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution, the Rajasthan and Karnataka laws, and the ILO and EU approaches. It finds that India now recognises gig workers but does not yet regulate algorithmic management itself. It proposes a rights-based framework built on notice, reasons, human review, appeal, interim protection and independent oversight, while leaving platforms free to act against genuine misconduct.

items.title: PRECISE: Reducing the bias of LLM evaluations using prediction‐powered ranking estimation
items.abstract: Abstract Evaluating the quality of search systems traditionally requires a significant number of human relevance annotations. In recent times, several systems have explored the usage of Large Language Models (LLMs) as automated judges for this task while their inherent biases prevent direct use for metric estimation. We present a statistical framework extending Prediction‐Powered Inference (PPI) (Angelopoulos, Duchi, and Zrnic 2024) that combines minimal human annotations with LLM judgments to produce reliable estimates of metrics which require sub‐instance annotations. Our method requires as few as 100 human‐annotated queries and 10,000 unlabeled examples, reducing annotation requirements by significantly compared to traditional approaches. We formulate our proposed framework ( PRECISE ) for inference of relevance uplift for an LLM‐based query reformulation application, extending PPI to sub‐instance annotations at the query‐document level. By reformulating the metric‐integration space, we reduced the computational complexity from to , where represents corpus size (in order of millions). Detailed experiments across prominent retrieval datasets demonstrate that our method reduces the variance of estimates for the business‐critical Precision@ K metric, while effectively correcting for LLM bias in low‐resource settings.

items.title: Predicting pandemics, predicting people: the ethical limits of AI-powered public health surveillance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming public health surveillance by enabling the integration of epidemiological, clinical, environmental, mobility, genomic, and digital data to detect emerging threats and anticipate disease transmission. However, the expansion from detecting outbreaks to predicting individual or group-level behaviors raises important ethical concerns related to privacy, autonomy, discrimination, transparency, accountability, and public trust. This mini-review examines the ethical limits of AI-powered public health surveillance, with particular attention to the transition from population-level epidemic prediction toward individual-level inference and profiling. It highlights how extensive data integration, algorithmic bias, unequal predictive errors, opaque models, and mission creep can undermine both equity and the legitimacy of surveillance systems. The review argues that predictive capability alone cannot establish ethical legitimacy. Instead, AI surveillance should be governed by necessity, proportionality, purpose limitation, data minimization, equity, transparency, meaningful human oversight, and mechanisms for accountability and redress. A lifecycle governance approach is further required to ensure continuous assessment of data quality, subgroup performance, model drift, unintended harms, and changing public-health needs. Ultimately, the ethical boundary of AI surveillance should be defined not by what can technically be predicted, but by what can be predicted and acted upon without compromising fundamental rights, equity, and public trust.

items.abstract: This chapter focuses on how artificial intelligence, IoT Analytics, and Behavioral Data Science can be used in the Hospitality 5.0 model for achieving personalized guest experience. As part of this effort, the Predictive Guest Experience Engineering (PGEE) approach relies on various sources of hospitality data ranging from guest booking behavior, IoT sensors in hotel rooms, guest mobile application usage, to guest reviews to create predictive models that can anticipate guest behavior. The chapter will make use of Hotel Reviews and Guest Behavior data set and employ exploratory data analysis techniques along with statistical hypothesis testing methods, and supervised machine learning models such as Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, XGBoost, and Multi-layered Neural Network. XGBoost yields the best accuracy rate of 92.7%, with AUC-ROC at 0.968, proving its effectiveness as the most efficient predictive model in the PGEE system. In this chapter, the PGEE system is introduced as an innovative concept, combining behavioral segmentation, predictive modeling, and personalization.

items.title: Predictive Maintenance for Bird Feeder Motors via Time-Series Current Analysis
items.abstract: Automated outdoor electronic device systems have been deployed widely for their high efficiency. However, environmental vulnerabilities could be a severe issue. To be more specific, high humidity outdoors causes feed agglomeration, therefore leading to fatal problems like mechanical jamming and motor burnout. According to current techniques, although deep learning model achieves the high accuracy of diagnosis, the heavy load is not suitable for a low-cost edge artificial intelligence (AI) controller. At the same time, traditional signal processing methods based on threshold values can easily cause false alarms in a noisy environment. This paper adopts lightweight sensorless predictive maintenance method, combining it with the motor current characteristic analysis (MCSA) and random forest classifier, and extracting the variance and peak amplitude features via Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) in the frequency domain. The result shows that by this method, the accuracy on the test data is up to 96.80%, which is superior to the standard deep neural network (89.30%) and maintains an extremely low inference latency, which is suitable for edge AI deployment.

items.title: Preregistration: Would US Adults on an Online Panel Donate Tissue for AI Training? A Four-Version Split-Ballot Survey
items.abstract: What this is A preregistration of a survey, published before any data were collected. It fixes the questions, hypotheses, exclusions, analysis code and decision rules in public before the pilot launches. Survey privacy notice: privacy-notice.pdf. This is the notice the survey introduction links to; the same text is part 4 of preregistration.pdf. Purpose Some consent forms for medical research, such as the Human Cell Atlas template, say donated tissue data may be used "for any purpose". The survey asks US adults whether they would agree to donate a small sample of tissue or cells for medical research when told the data could be used to train artificial intelligence (AI) models, by whom, and with a one-year period of first use by companies. Design A four-version split ballot. Each respondent is assigned at random to one description of how the data could be used: by university and hospital researchers by university and hospital researchers to train AI models by companies to train AI models by companies to train AI models, with only those companies able to use the data for the first year, after which it is made available to the public The question that follows is word for word the same in all four versions. An attention check comes first; four follow-up questions and four background questions come after. 10 questions in all. Sample US adults 18 and over in the Pollfish online panel (panel vendor: Pollfish LLC). An opt-in panel, not a probability sample. items.title: Projected Primal–Dual Gradient Preference Optimization Under Category-Wise Split-Conformal Safety Constraints for Large Language Model Post-Training
items.abstract: Preference optimisation improves helpfulness, but a single aggregate safety penalty lets frequent harm categories dominate the objective while rare ones bear the residual risk. This paper models post-training as a vector-constrained programme: the pairwise preference loss is minimised under one risk tolerance per harm category. The solver is a projected primal–dual gradient recursion that prices each category by its own residual violation. For a nonconvex objective we bound three horizon-averaged residuals—primal stationarity, dual regret and the average constraint value—for the unbiased, unclipped recursion and a uniformly drawn iterate; the implemented recursion is compared empirically with a no-EMA, no-clipping form of itself. Certification stays separate from optimisation: on an untouched calibration split, a multiplicity-adjusted fixed-sequence test gives release thresholds valid for all categories at once under correct category assignment, with an additive bound for learned routers. It certifies the scoring and filtering of corpus-distributed candidate responses, not text the trained policy generates. In one exploratory setting—one Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct backbone, PKU-SafeRLHF, three seeds—the recursion meets the per-category tolerance that direct preference optimisation and scalar-constrained schemes violate, cutting the worst-category miss rate at the training threshold from 0.176 to 0.057 at unchanged preference accuracy. The certified operating point barely moves: most of the constraint’s effect is a score translation shared by the harmful and benign responses of a prompt, which calibration provably absorbs. Whether a training constraint holds and whether the deployed gate is safer are different questions.

items.title: Prompt Competence in Higher Education
items.abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence in higher education has changed how knowledge is accessed, created, and assessed. A key idea in this shift is prompt competence. It refers to the ability to design, refine, and interpret inputs for AI systems. This chapter explains the basic ideas behind prompt competence. It links the concept with digital literacy and critical thinking. It also discusses simple ways to include prompt-based learning in different courses. Teaching methods, assessment approaches, and real-life uses are explained. The chapter also looks at policy issues such as ethical use, academic honesty, data privacy, and institutional rules. It connects theory with practice and policy. It offers clear guidance for educators and institutions to use AI in a responsible way and support future-ready learners.

items.title: Prompt Literacy as a Pedagogical Resource
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education is reshaping teaching, learning, and assessment practices. Within this evolving landscape, prompt literacy, the ability to design, refine, and critically evaluate prompts for AI systems, has emerged as a crucial yet underexplored competency. This chapter conceptualizes prompt literacy as a pedagogical resource within the Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) framework. It argues that while AI introduces new cognitive, pedagogical, and ethical demands, prompt literacy functions as a key resource that helps mitigate these challenges and enhances engagement, teaching effectiveness, and learning outcomes. Drawing on insights from digital literacy, AI literacy, and educational theory, the chapter develops a multidimensional understanding of prompt literacy. It also highlights implications for curriculum design, faculty development, and institutional policy, positioning prompt literacy as a strategic capability for fostering responsible and sustainable AI-enabled education.

items.title: Prompt-Based Cognitive Scaffolding
items.abstract: While research on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and prompt literacy has expanded rapidly, an integrated framework explaining prompt-mediated learning remains underdeveloped. We introduce the Prompt-Based Cognitive Scaffolding (PBCS) model, which conceptualizes prompts as regulatory mechanisms that coordinate cognitive, epistemic, and metacognitive processes during human–AI interaction. Building on cognitive scaffolding, distributed cognition, epistemic cognition, and prompt literacy, PBCS explains learning as a recursive coordination process in which human reasoning and AI-generated outputs are continuously refined. The model is operationalized through three interacting scaffolding dimensions and a functional prompt typology. Its explanatory scope is demonstrated across seminar-based learning, academic writing, collaborative learning, and research-oriented inquiry. We provide a theoretical foundation for understanding recursive human–AI knowledge construction.
